claims.text: The identity of X governs protective-oxide formation and stability in CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C.
In CrFeCoNiAl, preferential oxidation of Al produces an alumina-rich oxide scale.
The alumina-rich scale on CrFeCoNiAl is coherent, adherent, and slow-growing.
Oxides formed on CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn have poorer lattice matching with the metallic matrix than the oxide formed on CrFeCoNiAl.
Oxides formed on CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn have greater thermal-expansion mismatch with the substrate than the oxide formed on CrFeCoNiAl.
Lattice and thermal-expansion mismatch generate stresses that cause oxide cracking and spallation.
The high affinity of Al for oxygen drives formation of the proposed alumina-rich scale.
Scale composition, microstructure, lattice coherence, and substrate adhesion mediate whether the scale remains stable or cracks and spalls.
Under identical high-temperature exposure, CrFeCoNiAl will form a more stable, adherent, and slow-growing scale than CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn.
CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn will exhibit oxide cracking, delamination, or spallation after exposure.
Failure to form a protective layer is associated with rapid oxide growth, poor adherence, and spallation.
The proposed comparison applies to single-phase or multiphase CrFeCoNiX metallic solid solutions with X equal to Al, Si, or Mn.
The proposed exposure boundary is above 900 °C in an oxidizing or corrosive atmosphere.
Powder metallurgy or spark-plasma sintering can be used to control the initial microstructural state for the comparison.
A comparison of oxide thickness, growth rate, phase composition, interface coherence, adhesion, cracking, and spallation can test the proposed mechanism.
